posts.title: The Death Notice of Eamonn McCarty Review
posts.description: By Will Barber Taylor Death and all it means to us can be a difficult subject to tackle in any film, especially a short one. Death can often be humorous depending on the way it is handled – we find as much light and laughter in bleak as in the truly life affirming. To get this balance right relies on a great deal of skill and flair from writers and directors. This is most certainly the case in The Death Notice of Eamonn McCarty which finds humour in the absurd but also shows how life, even at its bleakest point, can lead to moments of joy and finding purpose in life. The wonderful interplay between Hannah Mamalis as Geraldine, desperate to make a positive impression on her first call and Michael McElhatton as the titular Eamonn McCarty, unable to process the reality of his shortened life span and the absurd way he has found out. posts.title: Nostalgie Review
posts.description: By Will Barber Taylor Drew Lord Haig (Aiden Gillen), a washed-up ’80s one-hit-wonder turned IT entrepreneur, is stunned when a Belfast battalion invites him to perform at their centenary celebration. Flattered and intrigued, Drew accepts, hoping to relive his glory days and recapture his youth. When he discovers the truth, he realizes that nostalgia can be as destructive as it can be a haven… If, as Roxy Music once sang, Love is the drug then nostalgia is a drug that is as lethal. We live in an age of nostalgia one in which people are desperate to, for good or ill, relive the triumphs and tragedies of the past. In Nostalgie, director Kathryn Ferguson and writer Stacey Gregg have created a truly prophetic tale of the curse and pain of that nostalgia. Set against the backdrop of the Troubles, Nostalgie emphasises how a love of the past and of past glories can mean something far darker and more sinister to some people than others. posts.title: Paper Plane Review
posts.description: By Will Barber Taylor Depicting childhood and in particular the complex mixture of joy, heartbreak and sadness that often colours it can be a difficult task for any director to truly capture. We are often compelled to see childhood as black or white, either filled with unabashed innocence and happiness at life or one filled with memories we would rather forget. Yet in Saoirse Ronan’s debut short film she perfectly captures the truth that many people experience complex childhoods that are both joyous and have moments of tension and sadness. There is in Ronan’s script a beautiful reality and sensitivity to her writing of the characters of Fay (Martha Malone) our central protagonist and her mother (Clare Dunne). Fay’s use of the titular paper planes to communicate has a real poetical beauty to it – as they soar through the air, they represent Fay’s hope, dreams and fears. Ronan’s ability to convey so much through the visual language of film speaks to her understanding of film as a medium.
